newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo stocks can't shake post-election blues.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stocks can't shake post-election blues.

text.p: Tokyo stocks fell for a fourth consecutive session on Thursday as investors were unable to shake off post-election blues and regain confidence about the strength of the Japanese economy.
The key 225-issue Nikkei average has fallen almost three percent over the week so far.

"Sentiment has been rather glum since Japan's Lower House elections ended on Sunday and aggressive buying interest has been dampened by a lack of a concrete direction," said Akishige Ishikura, analyst at Dai-ichi Securities.
"Foreign investors are also sticking to net sell positions, which is scaring domestic investors," he added.
The Nikkei closed 78.66 points, or 0.37 percent, lower at 21,003.49 on Thursday. Turnover dwindled to 238 million shares, a little more than half the volume of a regular trading day.
The Nikkei has lost 608.81 points, or 2.82 percent, from its Friday close of 21,612.30 points.
Hopes that the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), the dominant partner in Japan's outgoing coalition government, would win an overall majority in the Lower House of parliament prompted buying last week.
When the LDP came up 12 seats short of a majority, the market's mood darkened as the prospect of a shaky new coalition framework chilled investor sentiment, brokers said.

"The election results were disappointing and on top of that, the August diffusion index showed uncertainty over economic recovery, casting more dark clouds over the market," said Hideaki Akimoto, chief strategist at Daiwa Institute of Research.
On Tuesday, the Economic Planning Agency said the August diffusion index for leading economic indicators fell below the the so-called boom-or-bust 50 mark for the first time since March.
In addition to uncertain policies and doubts over economic recovery, domestic institutional investors were opting to invest in bonds rather than stocks, Akimoto added.
The key December Japanese government bond futures contract has set an all-time high for two days in a row, reaching a high for any benchmark contract of 124.42 on Friday.
"The Tokyo market is falling into a vicious circle," he said. "Domestic investors are keeping a vigilant eye on foreign investors, who are actually watching them for cues."
Brokers added that the collapse of financing company Nichiei Finance Co Ltd earlier this week, the largest insolvency case in Japan in the post-war period, also spread gloom.
Market sources said investors hoped the market would brighten after the the new coalition government cranks into action and starts pushing measures to stimulate the economy.
"Despite the dull market sentiment, some investment trusts and public funds are still bargain-hunting so a free-fall shouldn't occur," said Kenzo Doi, a strategist at Kokusai Securities.
"It won't sink, but it won't rise either and will wander within a 20,500 to 21,500 range for the time being," he said.
